lessons.title: Bridge grammar: word classes and expanded noun phrases
lessons.bigQuestion: How do adjectives and prepositions turn a plain noun into a picture?
objectives: To name nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs in a sentence
successCriteria: All: identify nouns, verbs and adjectives
Most: write expanded noun phrases with two adjectives
Some: add a prepositional phrase (with sharp claws, on the branch)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: describing the beauty and power of creation

keywords.def: a naming word for a person, place, animal or thing
a doing or being word
a word that describes a noun
a word that tells how, when or where a verb happens
a noun with extra describing words, like the hungry grey wolf

hook.text: Which word is the odd one out?
hook.a: pounced: it is a verb. The others are adjectives.

pictures.alt: a golden eagle, for an expanded noun phrase

resources: Display: word classes poster (school English displays)
Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 1: Capital letters and end marks) for pupils who need extra punctuation support

starter.a: noun (it can also be a verb: to claw)
verb (it can also be a noun: a hunt)

starter.q: Give an adjective for an owl

teach.heading: Four word classes
teach.note: Sort words in a card sort.

teach.heading: Expanded noun phrases
bullets: add adjectives: the hungry grey wolf
add a preposition: the hungry grey wolf in the forest
teach.note: Build the phrase step by step. A preposition shows where or when (in, on, under, behind).

teach.heading: Model
teach.note: Think aloud: which adjectives help the reader see this animal?

steps: Choose two adjectives: the patient, scaly crocodile
Add a prepositional phrase: under the muddy water
Put it in a sentence
Capital letter and full stop
model.answer: The patient, scaly crocodile waited under the muddy water.

teach.heading: Commas between adjectives
teach.note: Two adjectives of the same kind often take a comma.

misconception.right: the sleek, shiny black panther (choose two or three that add new detail)

teach.heading: Hinge: which is expanded?
teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: Which is an expanded noun phrase?
options: the long green snake on the rock
check.why: B has adjectives and a prepositional phrase around the noun snake. A is a plain noun phrase; C is a verb phrase.

practice.q: Underline the adjectives: The sly red fox crept past.
practice.a: sly, red
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: sly, red

practice.q: Find the adverb: The owl flew silently.
practice.a: silently

practice.q: Expand: the shark
practice.a: For example: the huge grey shark with sharp teeth

practice.q: Add a prepositional phrase: the spider ___
practice.a: For example: the spider in the corner of the web

independent.q: Core: expand four nouns (eagle, lion, frog, bat) with two adjectives each
independent.a: For example: the golden, powerful eagle
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: For example: the golden, powerful eagle

independent.q: Extend: add a prepositional phrase to each and write two as sentences
independent.a: For example: The powerful golden eagle on the cliff watched the valley.

independent.q: Stretch: write a three-sentence description of a predator using an adverb in each
independent.a: For example: The tiger moved silently. It waited patiently. Then it pounced suddenly.

exit.a: For example: the huge brown bear by the river

lessons.homework: Write five expanded noun phrases about animals you see this week (a pet, a bird, an insect). Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded word class cards (noun blue, adjective green); adjective bank. EAL: picture cards for each predator. Stretch: use a relative clause: the eagle, which nests on cliffs, ...

lessons.title: Verbs and tense: present perfect
objectives: Recognise simple past and present tense verbs
Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) correctly

keywords.def: a word that shows an action, state or event
shows when something happens
has/have + past participle, such as I have eaten
a verb that does not add -ed in the past

starter: Bismillah. Is this past or present: She walks to school?
Write the past tense of: jump, play, carry
Underline the verb: The children read quietly.

teach.heading: Verbs and tense
bullets: Verbs tell us what is happening
Present: I walk. Past: I walked.
teach.note: Ask pupils to act out verbs. Establish that every sentence needs a verb. Revise: add -ed for most past tense verbs, but remember spelling changes such as carry to carried.

teach.heading: Irregular past tense
teach.note: Say each verb and its past tense in a chant. Misconception: 'goed' and 'eated'. Explain that these verbs are irregular and have to be learnt, so we practise them often.

teach.heading: The present perfect
bullets: Pattern: have or has + past participle
teach.note: Explain that the present perfect links the past to now: 'I have finished' means the work is done now. Use a time line. Contrast with simple past: 'I finished my work yesterday.' The simple past names a finished time; the present perfect does not.

teach.heading: Past participles that change
bullets: Wrong: I have went. Right: I have gone.
teach.note: Choral practice. Write 'I seen' and 'I have went' on the board as common errors in speech and ask pupils to correct them. Explain that Standard English uses the participle after have/has.

teach.heading: Choosing the tense
bullets: We have visited the park three times (present perfect)
teach.note: Give clue words: yesterday, last week mean simple past; already, just, so far suggest present perfect. Ask for oral sentences with each clue.

practice: Change to the past tense: I go, we see, they write
Fill the gap: She has ___ (eat) her dinner.
Correct: I have went to the shop.
independent: Complete ten sentences using the correct form of the verb in brackets (e.g. He has ___ (take) the book).
Write five sentences of your own using has or have + a past participle.
Find and correct three errors: I seen a bird. She have wrote a card. We has gone home.
exit: Write the present perfect of the verb eat with 'she'.
Correct: I have saw the sea.
lessons.homework: Write four sentences about what you have done today, using have or has.
lessons.send: SEND: use a table with verb, past, participle. EAL: practise with gestures and flash cards. Stretch: explain in a sentence the difference between I ate and I have eaten.

lessons.title: Grammar: conjunctions when, before, after, while and because
lessons.bigQuestion: How do conjunctions show time and cause in my report?
objectives: To use the conjunctions when, before, after, while and because to join clauses
successCriteria: All: join two clauses with when or because
Most: use all five conjunctions correctly
Some: move the conjunction to the start and add the comma
lessons.smsc: Social: taking turns on play equipment (while one plays, another waits)

keywords.def: a word that joins words or clauses
a group of words with a verb
a clause that needs another clause to make sense, like because it is safe
a clause that makes sense on its own

hook.text: Which word is not a conjunction?
hook.a: slide: it is a noun or verb. The others join clauses.

resources: Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 1: Capital letters and end marks (for comma after an opening clause)) for pupils who need extra punctuation support

starter.q: Join with because: The slide is fast. It is steep.
starter.a: The slide is fast because it is steep.
A group of words with a verb

teach.heading: Time and cause
teach.note: Introduce the slide and check pupils are ready.

teach.heading: Main and subordinate clause
teach.note: The subordinate clause needs the main clause.

model.problem: The roundabout spins when you push it.
steps: Main clause: The roundabout spins (makes sense alone)
Conjunction: when
Subordinate clause: you push it
Check: "when you push it" alone does not make sense

teach.heading: Move it to the front
teach.note: Comma after the subordinate clause when it comes first.

misconception.wrong: When you push it the roundabout spins.
misconception.right: When you push it, the roundabout spins.

teach.heading: Hinge: which conjunction?
teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: Check the ropes ___ you climb the frame.
check.why: before shows the order: check first, then climb.

practice.q: Join with while: One child swings. Another waits.
practice.a: One child swings while another waits.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: One child swings while another waits.

practice.q: Join with after: Wipe the slide. It rains.
practice.a: Wipe the slide after it rains.

practice.q: Move to the front with a comma: The zip wire stops when it reaches the end.
practice.a: When it reaches the end, the zip wire stops.

independent.q: Core: write five sentences about your play equipment, one with each conjunction (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.a: For example: The slide is safe because it has high sides.
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (The roundabout spins when you push it.): Main clause: The roundabout spins (makes sense alone) | Conjunction: when | Subordinate clause: you push it | Check: "when you push it" alone does not make sense | Result: Main clause + conjunction + subordinate clause.

independent.q: Extend: start two sentences with the conjunction and add the comma
independent.a: For example: Before you slide, sit down.

independent.q: Stretch: write one sentence with two conjunctions
independent.a: For example: When it rains, the slide is slippery because the water reduces friction.

exit.q: Add a comma: Because it is metal the frame is strong.
exit.a: Because it is metal, the frame is strong.

lessons.homework: Write three sentences about your journey to a park or shop using when, before and after. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: clause cards to match and a conjunction strip. EAL: model sentences with one word changed. Stretch: use although: Although it is fast, the slide is safe.

lessons.title: Grammar: adverbs and prepositions for time, place and cause
lessons.bigQuestion: How do adverbs and prepositions make an explanation precise?
objectives: To use adverbs and prepositions to express time, place and cause
successCriteria: All: identify adverbs and prepositions in sentences
Most: use them to show time, place and cause
Some: start a sentence with an adverb or prepositional phrase and add a comma
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: precise language helps us describe Allah's creation truthfully

islamicLink.text: Precise language helps us describe Allah's creation truthfully

keywords.def: a word that tells how, when, where or why something happens
a word that shows where or when, like under or after
a preposition and the words after it, like under the table

hook.text: Which word is the odd one out?
hook.a: magnet: it is a noun. The others are prepositions.

resources: A magnet and paper clips (optional demonstration)

starter.q: Find the adverb: The spinner slowly stopped.
Give a How or Why title about magnets
starter.a: For example: How Do Magnets Work?

teach.heading: Time, place, cause
teach.note: Introduce the slide and check pupils are ready.

teach.heading: Model: precise explanation sentences
teach.note: Demonstrate with a magnet on camera.

steps: Place: The clip moves across the table.
Time: Soon, the clip moves across the table.
Cause: Because of the magnet, the clip moves across the table.
Comma after the opening phrase
model.answer: Soon, because of the magnet, the clip slides across the table.

teach.heading: Fronted phrases need a comma
teach.note: When the phrase starts the sentence.

misconception.wrong: After a few seconds the spinner stops.
misconception.right: After a few seconds, the spinner stops.

teach.heading: Hinge: which shows place?
teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: Which phrase shows place?
check.why: under the magnet tells us where. A shows time; C shows cause.

practice.q: Add a preposition of place: The pins stick ___ the magnet.
practice.a: For example: to, under
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: For example: to, under

practice.q: Add an adverb of time: ___, the parachute opens.
practice.a: For example: Then, Soon

practice.q: Front the phrase: The toy slows because of friction.
practice.a: Because of friction, the toy slows.

independent.q: Core: write five sentences about forces, each with an adverb or preposition showing time, place or cause (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.a: For example: Inside the toy, a spring stores energy.
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (The clip moves.): Place: The clip moves across the table. | Time: Soon, the clip moves across the table. | Cause: Because of the magnet, the clip moves across the table. | Comma after the opening phrase | Result: Soon, because of the magnet, the clip slides across the table.

independent.q: Extend: label each one T, P or C
independent.a: Labels match the phrases used

independent.q: Stretch: write a three-sentence explanation of why a ball stops rolling using all three jobs
independent.a: For example: After a few seconds, the ball slows down. Underneath it, the carpet rubs. Because of friction, it stops.

exit.q: Add the comma: Inside the box the magnet is hidden.
exit.a: Inside the box, the magnet is hidden.

lessons.homework: Write three sentences describing where things are in your room using prepositions. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: preposition cards with arrows and pictures. EAL: physical demonstration of under, between, inside. Stretch: use a subordinate clause and a prepositional phrase in one sentence.

lessons.title: Spelling: prefixes un-, dis-, mis-, re- and in-
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a prefix change the meaning of a word?
objectives: To add the prefixes un-, dis-, mis-, re- and in- to root words
successCriteria: All: add un- and re- correctly
Most: choose between un-, dis-, mis-, re- and in- and explain the meaning
Some: use prefixed words accurately in sentences about forces
lessons.smsc: Moral: re- words like rebuild and reuse: looking after things and not wasting

keywords.def: letters added to the start of a word to change its meaning
the word you start with
mean not or the opposite
means again or back
means wrongly

hook.text: appear, disappear, reappear. What do dis- and re- do to appear?
hook.a: dis- makes the opposite; re- means again.

resources: Vocabulary Intervention Programme (Lesson 10: Prefixes: meaning at the front) for pupils who need extra vocabulary support

teach.heading: Prefixes
teach.note: A prefix never changes the spelling of the root: dis + appear = disappear (one s, one p).

teach.heading: Keep the root
teach.note: Just add the prefix.

teach.heading: Model
teach.note: Think aloud about meaning.

model.problem: The magnet stopped working. Use a prefix word.
steps: Root: connect
Meaning needed: the opposite
Choose dis-: disconnect
Sentence: The wire was disconnected.

teach.heading: Hinge: which prefix?
teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: Which word means "build again"?
check.why: re- means again. un- and mis- do not fit and are not real words here.

practice.q: Add a prefix to make the opposite: visible
practice.a: invisible
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: invisible

practice.q: Add a prefix: spell (wrongly)
practice.a: misspell

practice.q: Add a prefix: charge (again)
practice.a: recharge

practice.q: Add a prefix: agree (not)
practice.a: disagree

independent.q: Core: add the right prefix to ten words: lock, appear, correct, use, behave, fair, connect, wind, visible, tidy (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.a: unlock, disappear, incorrect, reuse, misbehave, unfair, disconnect, rewind, invisible, untidy
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: unlock, disappear, incorrect, reuse, misbehave, unfair, disconnect, rewind, invisible, untidy

independent.q: Extend: write three sentences about magnets or toys using prefixed words
independent.a: For example: The magnet is invisible inside the toy.

independent.q: Stretch: find two words where in- is not a prefix (inside, insect) and explain
independent.a: In inside and insect, in is part of the word, not a prefix meaning not.

lessons.homework: Learn ten prefix words (unlock, disappear, incorrect, reuse, misbehave, unfair, disconnect, rewind, invisible, untidy) for a quick check. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: five words only, prefix cards to place in front of root cards. EAL: picture opposites (lock/unlock). Stretch: find prefixes il-, im-, ir- (illegal, impossible, irregular).

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Reading a fable: The Hare and the Tortoise
objectives: Describe the features of a fable
Retrieve and explain information from a short text

keywords.def: a short story with animal characters that teaches a lesson
the lesson a story teaches
a person or animal in a story
find information in a text

starter: Bismillah. Name one conjunction and use it in a sentence.
What does the prefix mis- mean?
Write an expanded noun phrase about a river.

teach.heading: What is a fable?
bullets: A short story with a lesson
A fable ends with a moral
Aesop is the best-known writer of fables
teach.note: Introduce fables as very old stories told to teach good behaviour. Ask pupils which stories with animals they know. Explain that the animals have one main quality, such as pride or kindness.

teach.heading: Read the fable
bullets: The hare boasts about his speed
They race to the oak tree
The hare naps; the tortoise keeps going
teach.note: Aesop's fable, retold: A hare laughed at a tortoise for being so slow. 'I could win any race with my eyes closed,' he boasted. 'Then let us race,' said the tortoise quietly. A fox marked the finish line at the old oak tree. 'Ready, steady, go!' The hare shot off and was soon far ahead. Looking back, he saw that the tortoise had hardly moved. 'I have plenty of time,' he yawned, and lay down under a tree for a nap. The tortoise plodded on, step by step, and never stopped. When the hare woke, the sun was low. He sprinted towards the oak tree, but the tortoise was already crossing the line. Moral: slow and steady wins the race. Read aloud with expression. Pause after the boast and ask pupils to predict what will happen.

teach.heading: Find the facts
bullets: Quote the text to prove it
teach.note: Model retrieval: find a sentence that answers 'Who marked the finish line?' Show how to scan for key words and underline the answer. Remind pupils to answer in a sentence.

teach.heading: Why did the tortoise win?
bullets: Boasting led to the hare's mistake
teach.note: Ask for answers starting 'The tortoise won because...'. Accept reasons from the text: the hare slept. Model a full sentence answer.

teach.heading: The moral
bullets: Slow and steady wins the race
The lesson is shown by what happens
teach.note: Ask the class to explain the moral in their own words. Link to Islam: the Prophet (peace be upon him) is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim to have said that the most beloved deeds to Allah are those done regularly, even if small. Keep the link brief and respectful.

practice: Who marked the finish line?
Find and copy one word that shows the tortoise moved slowly.
What did the hare do instead of racing?
independent: Answer in full sentences: (a) What did the hare boast? (b) Where was the finish line? (c) Why was the hare late? (d) What is the moral?
Draw a story map with four boxes: boast, race, nap, finish.
List three features of a fable using the story as evidence.
exit: Write the moral of the fable.
Who is the main character who makes a mistake?
lessons.homework: Retell the fable to a family member and write the moral on a card.
lessons.send: SEND: read the story with a partner; give picture sequencing cards. EAL: pre-teach boasted, plodded, sprinted. Stretch: suggest another moral and defend it.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Characters and inference
objectives: Use evidence from the text to say what a character is like
Explain the meaning of words in context

keywords.def: work out something that the author does not say directly
words from the text that prove your idea
spoke proudly about what you can do
walked slowly and heavily

starter: Bismillah. What is a fable?
What is the moral of The Hare and the Tortoise?
Find the verb: The tortoise plodded on.

teach.heading: Inference
bullets: Authors do not tell us everything
We use clues to work it out
I think... because the text says...
teach.note: Show a picture of a child holding an umbrella and ask what the weather is. Explain that we use clues. Reading is detective work: we find evidence in the text to support our ideas.

teach.heading: What was the hare like?
bullets: He thought he had plenty of time: overconfident
teach.note: Reread the fable and underline clues about the hare. Model a full answer: 'I think the hare was proud because he said he could win with his eyes closed.' Ask pupils to find another.

teach.heading: What was the tortoise like?
bullets: He plodded on and never stopped: determined
teach.note: Contrast the tortoise's quiet reply with the hare's boast. Ask which character we should copy. Link to humility as a value we admire in Islam, without making false claims about texts.

teach.heading: Words in context
teach.note: Show how neighbouring words help with meaning: 'plodded on, step by step'. Ask pupils to replace each word with a simpler one and check it still makes sense.

teach.heading: Write an inference answer
bullets: Evidence: he lay down for a nap
Explain: he forgot the race was still going
teach.note: Model a P.E.E. style answer: Point, Evidence, Explain. Keep it simple for Year 3. Ask for sentence starters: 'This shows that...'

practice: How do you know the tortoise was determined?
Which word shows how the hare ran at the end?
What does plodded tell us about the tortoise?
independent: Write two sentences about the hare using 'I think... because...' with a quotation.
Write two sentences about the tortoise in the same way.
Choose a new adjective for each character and prove it with evidence.
exit: Complete: I think the hare was careless because...
lessons.homework: Write a character description of the hare using three adjectives and evidence.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters and highlighted evidence. EAL: act the words boasted and plodded. Stretch: compare how the hare feels at the start and end.

lessons.title: Bridge grammar: punctuating direct speech
lessons.bigQuestion: How do inverted commas show the reader exactly who is speaking?
objectives: To punctuate direct speech with inverted commas
successCriteria: All: put inverted commas around the spoken words
Most: punctuate speech with a comma or question mark inside the inverted commas
Some: start a new line for a new speaker and vary the speech verb
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: polite conversation and good manners (adab)
lessons.smsc: Social: speaking kindly; the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that a good word is charity

islamicLink.text: Speaking kindly; the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that a good word is charity

keywords.def: the exact words a character says
speech marks that go around spoken words
words that say who spoke, like said Amir
the verb in the speech tag, like asked or whispered

hook.text: Lets eat Grandma! Lets eat, Grandma! One mark changes everything. What does punctuation do?
hook.a: It changes the meaning: punctuation helps the reader understand exactly what is meant (and who is spoken to).

pictures.find: dinner table set with plates photograph
pictures.alt: a table set for a meal (polite conversation)

resources: Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 5: Quotation marks and dialogue) for pupils who need extra punctuation support

starter.q: Make it imperative: You can sit down.
Add a capital and end mark: where is my bag

teach.heading: What is direct speech?
teach.note: Show a speech bubble, then the same words as a sentence with inverted commas.

teach.heading: The rules
teach.note: Model the order: open, words, punctuation, close, tag.

steps: Open inverted commas
Capital letter for the first spoken word
Spoken words, then ? or , inside
Close inverted commas
Speech tag: asked Yusuf.

teach.heading: Comma, not full stop
teach.note: If the tag comes after, use a comma inside, not a full stop.

teach.heading: New speaker, new line
bullets: Each new speaker starts a new line
teach.note: Show a short dialogue laid out correctly. Point out each new line.

teach.heading: Hinge: which is correct?
teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: Which is punctuated correctly?
check.why: A has the comma inside the inverted commas before the tag. B has no comma; C puts the inverted commas round the wrong words.

practice.q: Punctuate: can I have some water asked Zara
practice.a: "Can I have some water?" asked Zara.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: "Can I have some water?" asked Zara.

practice.q: Punctuate: thank you said Musa
practice.a: "Thank you," said Musa.

practice.q: Choose a better verb than said: "Watch out!" ___ Bilal.
practice.a: For example: shouted

independent.q: Core: punctuate five sentences of direct speech (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.a: For example: "It is time to go," said Dad.
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: For example: "It is time to go," said Dad.

independent.q: Extend: write a four-line polite conversation at a dinner table, new speaker new line
independent.a: For example: "Bismillah," said Mum. "Please pass the rice," asked Adam.

independent.q: Stretch: put the speech tag first: Mum said, "..."
independent.a: For example: Grandad smiled and said, "That was delicious."

exit.q: Punctuate: where are my shoes asked Ibrahim
What do you do when a new person speaks?

lessons.homework: Write a short polite conversation between two friends sharing food, with every line punctuated correctly. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: speech punctuation checklist with the 66 99 shapes; complete two, not five. EAL: model sentences to copy and change one word. Stretch: break the speech in the middle: "When we finish," said Mum, "we will read."

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Planning our own fable
objectives: Choose characters, a flaw and a moral
Plan a fable in five parts

keywords.def: a weakness in a character, such as greed or pride
the trouble that happens in the story
how the problem is solved
a short outline of what will happen

starter: Bismillah. What is a moral?
Add inverted commas: Come with me said the fox.
Use the word because in a sentence.

teach.heading: What makes a good fable?
bullets: A problem caused by that flaw
A clear moral at the end
teach.note: Reread the main features from lesson 6. Ask pupils to name flaws: pride, greed, laziness, dishonesty. Explain that the moral should come from what happens, not just be added at the end.

teach.heading: Choose a moral first
teach.note: Link morals to values such as honesty and kindness. Select one together. Moral first means the whole plan works backwards from the lesson, which makes the ending meaningful.

teach.heading: A model plan
bullets: Characters: Sami the squirrel, Mrs Owl
Problem: he hides too many nuts
Moral: take only what you need
teach.note: Model: Sami the squirrel gathers far more nuts than he needs. Winter comes and he cannot carry the nuts home; other animals share and he learns to share too. Build the plan in five boxes: opening, build-up, problem, resolution, moral.

teach.heading: Five-part plan
bullets: Opening: meet the characters and setting
Build-up: the flaw begins to cause trouble
teach.note: Show an empty five-box grid. Pupils choose characters, setting, flaw and moral and write short notes in each box. Remind them to use notes, not full sentences.

teach.heading: Plan with detail
bullets: Choose two good adjectives for each character
Note a conjunction or adverb for each part
teach.note: Prompt pupils to think of language from Unit 1 for their plan: an expanded noun phrase for the setting and one line of dialogue.

practice: Match each flaw to a moral: pride, greed, dishonesty / honesty is best, take only what you need, be humble.
Name two animal characters and one adjective for each.
Where will your fable happen?
independent: Complete a five-part plan for your own fable.
Write one line of speech you will use.
Write two expanded noun phrases for your setting and main character.

starter.q: What does as a result mean?

teach.heading: Linking cause and effect
teach.note: Introduce the slide and check pupils are ready.

head: Connective
Use
Example
rows: As a result, it lands gently.

teach.heading: Model: one paragraph
teach.note: Write live from the spinner plan.

steps: As the spinner turns, its point rubs against the table.
This creates friction, which acts against the spin.
As a result, the spinner slows down and begins to wobble.
Therefore, it soon falls onto its side.

teach.heading: Do not overuse
teach.note: Vary connectives.

misconception.wrong: It spins so it rubs so it slows so it stops.
misconception.right: It spins and rubs on the table. As a result, it slows. Therefore, it soon stops.

teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: The magnet is strong. ___, it lifts five pins.
check.why: As a result introduces the effect. Because would need a different sentence order; before shows time.
